titles: You're in the Global 1%. Why Doesn't It Feel Like It?
The World Got Radically More Equal. Your Country Didn't.
The Elephant Curve: Why 1.3 Billion Escaped Poverty And You Got Nothing
primary_title: You're in the Global 1%. Why Doesn't It Feel Like It?
description:
Global inequality has been falling for thirty years, the fastest collapse in poverty since the Industrial Revolution. So why does almost everyone in the rich world feel poorer? Both facts live on the same chart.

We animate the entire world income distribution from 1800 to today. In 1975 humanity had two distinct humps: a poor world and a rich world. By 2015 those humps had fused into one. Then we zoom into the far right tail, find where you actually sit, and draw the elephant curve that explains why the Western working and lower-middle class gained almost nothing during the greatest poverty reduction in human history.

CHAPTERS
00:00 Introduction & The Intuition Trap
00:02 The Historical Inflection Point
00:05 The Data Divergence
00:09 The 2030 Horizon & Conclusion

KEY STATISTICAL TAKEAWAYS
• Extreme poverty fell from roughly 38% of humanity in 1990 to under 10% today, and the global interpersonal Gini dropped from about 0.70 to the low 0.60s, the first sustained decline since the Industrial Revolution.
• Within-country inequality moved the opposite direction almost everywhere: the US top 1% wealth share rose from roughly 24% in 1989 to around 31% today.
• The flattest real income growth from 1988 to 2008 did not belong to the world's poor. It belonged to the 80th to 90th global percentile, the Western working and lower-middle class. That is the trunk of the elephant.

SOURCES & METHODOLOGY
Data compiled from the World Bank Poverty and Inequality Platform (PIP), the World Inequality Database (WID.world), Branko Milanovic's global household survey work on the elephant curve, Our World in Data income distribution series, the Maddison Project historical GDP estimates, and the Luxembourg Income Study. All incomes are expressed in purchasing power parity terms and adjusted for inflation, so cross-country and cross-century comparisons reflect real consumption rather than exchange rates. Global inequality figures rely on household surveys of differing quality and coverage, so Gini estimates carry meaningful uncertainty bands and different researchers reach slightly different levels while agreeing on the direction of travel. Pre-1950 distributions are reconstructions, not measurements. Percentile placement is based on global income distribution after tax and transfers.
